title: What to expect at your first physiotherapy appointment

body:
Starting physiotherapy can feel uncertain if you have not done it before. Knowing what happens in the first session makes it easier to prepare and to get the most from your time.

## Before you come

A little preparation helps. Think about what you would like to achieve, whether that is walking further, returning to a sport or simply sleeping comfortably. It also helps to wear clothes you can move in.

- Wear comfortable, loose clothing
- Have a list of any medication you take
- Bring any scan results or letters you have
- Write down your main questions and goals

## The conversation

The first part of an initial assessment is mostly talking. You will be asked about your symptoms, how they started, what makes them better or worse, your general health and what matters most to you. There is no need to prepare a perfect summary; the questions guide you.

## The physical assessment

Next comes an assessment of how you move. This may include watching simple movements, checking strength and range of motion, and gently examining the area. You will be told what is being done and can stop or ask questions at any point.

## Explanation and plan

You should leave understanding what is likely to be going on, what the next steps are and what you can do yourself. That often includes a few exercises to start, advice on activity, and a suggestion for follow-up sessions. Initial assessments at Body Function last 50 minutes, with follow-ups of 30 minutes.

## Home visits

If your appointment is at home, it helps to have a clear space with room to move and, if possible, a chair and a floor area. Availability and travel coverage are confirmed before booking.

## Key points

- The first session is mostly listening, assessing and explaining
- You are encouraged to ask questions at any point
- You should leave with a clear next step

## When to seek help

If your symptoms are severe, sudden or rapidly worsening, or you are worried about your health, contact your GP, call NHS 111 or seek emergency care instead of waiting for an appointment.

This article is general information and is not a substitute for an individual assessment or medical advice.
